arXiv:2608.08315v1 [cs.CV] 08 Aug 2026

Your VLM Already Knows When: Training-Free Temporal Grounding by Asking Yes or No

Ji Huang Affiliation: Queen’s University Belfast Email: jhuang28@qub.ac.uk    Barry Devereux Affiliation: Queen’s University Belfast Email: B.Devereux@qub.ac.uk    Hui Wang Affiliation: Queen’s University Belfast Email: h.wang@qub.ac.uk
Abstract

Multimodal LLMs that recognise events reliably still fail to say when they happen. Prompted for timestamps, strong VLMs reach as little as 3.8%3.8\% R@0.5 on Charades-STA, and 7777 to 80%80\% of their wrong predictions carry low output entropy: the models are confidently wrong, and entropy-based error detection stays below a random classifier. We show that this failure lives in the task interface, not in perception. Holding the weights fixed, replacing timestamp regression with a coarse-to-fine scan of binary questions, whose first-token probabilities are consumed only as a ranking, raises R@0.5 by 2828 to 5050 points across four frozen backbones. The residual failures decompose into two measurable axes: a perception axis that moves with the backbone, and a geometry axis that is analytically predictable from the ratio of the output-window and event widths. FV-Action, the training-free method built on this analysis, reaches 56.8%56.8\% R@0.5 on Charades-STA, above the same backbone’s native grounding pipeline and the strongest training-free result on this benchmark; it surpasses every TVG-trained model evaluated zero-shot on TACoS, and improves over direct prediction on ActivityNet Captions and QVHighlights, with no temporal supervision at any stage.

1 Introduction

Temporal video grounding (TVG) asks where in an untrimmed video the event described by a natural-language query occurs [7, 13, 23]. The task demands joint reasoning over visual content and language, precisely what multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are built for [3, 1], and the natural way to use one is to ask it for timestamps directly. This fails, and not marginally. InternVL2-8B [3], strong across diverse visual benchmarks, reaches 3.76%3.76\% R@0.5 on Charades-STA [7] when prompted for timestamps. Models fine-tuned specifically for grounding fare little better (TimeChat [24] 31.2%31.2\%, LITA [11] 8.87%8.87\%), and the strongest general-purpose VLM under an optimised native temporal pipeline reaches 53.6%53.6\% [33]. The same pattern holds on ActivityNet Captions and TACoS. Why does direct timestamp prediction fail so systematically for models that excel at visual reasoning?

A natural hypothesis is that the models are guessing, in which case their own uncertainty should expose the errors. The opposite is true. Across TimeChat, LITA, and VTG-LLM, 7777 to 80%80\% of wrong predictions carry low output entropy: the models are confidently wrong. Entropy-based error detection reaches F1 below 0.360.36 on all three, under the 0.500.50 of a random classifier, so no amount of confidence thresholding separates right from wrong. The failure is systematic rather than epistemic, which points away from what the model knows and toward how it is asked to answer.

We test that reading directly. For each sample we compare the model’s Yes-probability on the ground-truth window against an equal-width, non-overlapping window from the same video, using the binary question “Does this clip show {query}?”, and summarise the outcome by the signal gap Δ=P⁡(Yes∣GT)−P⁡(Yes∣neg)\Delta=P(\text{Yes}\mid\text{GT})-P(\text{Yes}\mid\text{neg}) and the rate at which the ground-truth clip wins. On Charades-STA perception is intact (Δ=0.308\Delta=0.308; the true clip wins 80.5%80.5\% of pairs), and holding the model fixed while replacing timestamp regression with a coarse-to-fine scan over these questions (Sec. 3) raises R@0.5 from 3.763.76 to 53.3953.39 for InternVL2-8B and from 28.4128.41 to 56.7756.77 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Where the model perceives the event, the interface, not perception, is the bottleneck.

The failures that remain decompose along two measurable and separable axes, and this decomposition organises the paper. The perception axis is a property of the backbone. On TACoS the per-clip signal gap rises from 0.1860.186 (InternVL2) to 0.2600.260 (Qwen2.5-VL) on identical samples (p=0.0009p{=}0.0009), and deployed accuracy rises with it, which makes the gap a cheap pre-deployment diagnostic of which model will scan better. The geometry axis is a property of the output form. With a fixed window of width WW, overlap with an event of width gg cannot exceed min⁡(W,g)/max⁡(W,g)\min(W,g)/\max(W,g), so accuracy at a given threshold is predictable before any model runs; on ActivityNet the ground-truth buckets outside the feasible band collapse exactly as the bound dictates, even though the located peak still falls inside the event on up to 95%95\% of them. The two axes prescribe different remedies, a better instrument for one and a better output rule for the other, and neither is repaired by processing the scores in between: smoothing, contrastive correction, denser scanning, and prompt rewriting all leave the located peak where it was (Sec. 5).

The mechanism behind the interface gap is a format mismatch. Decimal timestamps conditioned on a language query are largely absent from pre-training corpora, so a model asked to emit them falls back on distributional priors and produces plausible values with high confidence, which is exactly the low-entropy failure observed above. Binary VQA sidesteps the missing format, and scanning consumes only the ranking of its answers across clips. Ranking is a weaker requirement than calibration, and it is the one the models meet: scores that look poorly calibrated in isolation still order clips reliably within a video (Sec. 3).

FV-Action operationalises this reading with deliberate simplicity. It poses one binary question per clip over a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of video segments, selects the peak by rank, and emits a fixed-width window; the backbone stays frozen and performs only the judgement it is demonstrably good at. On Charades-STA it reaches 56.8%56.8\% R@0.5, surpassing the same backbone’s optimised native pipeline (53.6%53.6\% [33]) on identical frozen weights, and doing so on the stricter R@0.7 as well (29.729.7 vs. 28.528.5). The gain is a property of the interface, not the model: it holds across four backbones with improvements of 2828 to 5050 points, including InternVL2-8B from ∼3.8%{\sim}3.8\% to 53.4%53.4\%. Without any temporal training, FV-Action remains competitive with systems that pay for it, whether by full supervision (UniVTG [19], 60.2%60.2\%), reinforcement learning (Time-R1 [25], 60.8%60.8\%), or large-scale annotation (OmniVTG [33], 63.2%63.2\% with 359359K pairs), and it improves over direct prediction on four benchmarks (Charades-STA, ActivityNet Captions [13], TACoS [23], and QVHighlights [15]).

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    A diagnostic study showing that 77–80% of MLLM temporal hallucinations are confident (low-entropy), with entropy-based error detection achieving F1 << 0.36 across TimeChat, LITA, and VTG-LLM, below the random-classifier baseline of 0.50. This establishes that the dominant failure mode is systematic format hallucination, not epistemic uncertainty.

  • •

    A controlled same-backbone comparison isolating the interface as the bottleneck. With weights, frames, and prompting held fixed, replacing timestamp regression with binary VQA scanning raises R@0.5 by 2828 to 5050 points on Charades-STA across four frozen backbones, and lifts Qwen2.5-VL-7B above its own native grounding pipeline on both R@0.5 and R@0.7.

  • •

    An analysis decomposing the residual failures into two measurable axes. The perception axis moves with the backbone. On TACoS the per-clip oracle gap rises from 0.1860.186 to 0.2600.260 when InternVL2 is replaced by Qwen2.5-VL, a paired difference on identical samples (p=0.0009p{=}0.0009), and deployed accuracy rises with it. The geometry axis is governed by the fit between the output window and the event width, and is analytically predictable from their ratio alone.

  • •

    FV-Action, a training-free grounding framework built on this analysis. It poses only binary questions to a frozen VLM and reads a ranking rather than a calibrated score, reaching 56.8%56.8\% R@0.5 on Charades-STA, the strongest training-free result on this benchmark, with consistent gains over direct prediction on ActivityNet Captions and TACoS.

2 Related Work

Supervised video temporal grounding.

Video temporal grounding (TVG) localises a natural-language query in a video as a [s,e][s,e] interval [7]. Span-based methods enumerate candidate moments and rank them with cross-modal similarity (2D-TAN [31]) or contrastive metric learning (MMN [27]). Proposal-free approaches directly regress start/end offsets from dense feature interactions (UniVTG [19]), achieving over 60%60\% R@0.5 on Charades-STA with full supervision. Despite strong in-domain performance, these models require complete TVG annotations and generalise poorly across domains without retraining. Our method requires no TVG annotations at any stage.

Multimodal LLMs for TVG.

Integrating temporal grounding into video LLMs has been pursued along several lines. LITA [11] and VTG-LLM [8] insert special timestamp tokens into the vocabulary so the model can emit temporal boundaries as part of its output sequence. TimeChat [24], VTimeLLM [10], ChatVTG [22], Momentor [21], and HawkEye [26] instead fine-tune on TVG instruction data, while Enrich-and-Detect [20] combines a VLM with an external proposal network. At larger training scales, TimeMarker [2], TRACE [9], TimeSuite [30], and UniTime [18] incorporate temporal annotations during pre-training to strengthen localisation. Despite these efforts, most models fall short of fully supervised specialists, partly because generating sub-second timestamps forces a vocabulary trained on natural language to operate as a numerical regressor. We show that this is a formulation bottleneck rather than a capacity bottleneck, in TVG-tuned and general-purpose models [3, 1, 29] alike: InternVL2-8B predicts timestamps at 3.76%3.76\% R@0.5 yet discriminates clips via binary VQA at AUROC 0.7820.782, and switching the interface recovers 2828 to 5050 pp across four frozen backbones (Table 6). Time-R1 [25] addresses the regression difficulty with reinforcement learning on 2,500 TVG samples, reaching 60.8%60.8\% R@0.5. Concurrently, OmniVTG [33] independently identifies the same formulation bottleneck and proposes a three-stage training pipeline (supervised fine-tuning, chain-of-thought fine-tuning, and GRPO reinforcement learning) on a proprietary dataset of 359,K temporal annotations spanning 2,124 hours, reaching 63.2%63.2\% R@0.5 on Charades-STA. FV-Action achieves 56.8%56.8\% with no training on TVG data, within striking distance of OmniVTG, showing that interface redesign alone captures the majority of the gain.

Zero-shot and training-free TVG.

LLM4VG [6] generates per-second captions and feeds them to an LLM for temporal reasoning, reaching 11.8%11.8\% R@0.5 on Charades-STA, only marginally above a random baseline, because language-space reasoning cannot substitute for direct visual evidence. Moment-GPT [28] assembles a multi-model pipeline combining language rewriting, video captioning, and LLM reasoning, reaching 38.4%38.4\%, while GranAlign [12] aligns visual granularities via CLIP matching and achieves 39.6%39.6\%, and BTDP [5] reaches 40.0%40.0\% with dense captioning and LLM alignment. FV-Action differs from all of these in that it directly queries a single VLM with binary visual questions at each candidate clip, requiring no caption generation and no auxiliary models. This reformulation raises the training-free Charades-STA R@0.5 to 56.8%56.8\%, a 16.816.8 pp improvement over the prior best (40.0%40.0\%).

Uncertainty as an error signal.

A parallel line asks whether a model’s own uncertainty exposes its errors. Semantic entropy detects confabulations in free-form text generation [14], and binary interrogation probes such as POPE [17] audit object hallucination in VLMs with yes-or-no questions.

Our diagnostic study carries this question to temporal grounding and returns a negative answer: across three TVG-tuned models, 7777 to 80%80\% of wrong predictions carry low output entropy, and entropy-based error detection stays below a random classifier (F1 <0.36<0.36). The failure is systematic rather than epistemic, so no confidence signal can gate it away; FV-Action instead replaces the unreliable self-report with direct visual evidence, the ranking of binary judgements over clips, which is itself a POPE-style interrogation turned into a localisation instrument.

3 Method

3.1 Problem Formulation

Given an untrimmed video VV of duration TT seconds and a natural-language query qq, temporal video grounding (TVG) seeks the interval [s,e]⊂[0,T][s,e]\subset[0,T] during which the described event occurs. Two interfaces can extract this interval from a multimodal LLM. Under the generative interface, the model is prompted to emit decimal timestamps directly. Under the discriminative interface, the model answers only a binary VQA question about a short clip, and localisation is performed by an external scan over clip positions. The same frozen backbone behaves very differently under the two. InternVL2-8B reaches 3.76 R@0.5 when generating timestamps, yet separates clips inside the ground-truth interval from equal-width non-overlapping negatives at a discrimination rate of 80.5% (Sec. 5); switching only the interface raises its R@0.5 to 53.39. Because the backbone is identical under the two interfaces and only the output format changes, this gap isolates the interface as the cause: the grounding ability is present but expressed through the wrong channel. The mechanism is a format mismatch. Decimal timestamps conditioned on a language query are largely absent from pre-training corpora, so the model falls back on language priors and produces plausible but ungrounded values, which is why these errors carry low entropy (Sec. 1). FV-Action is the discriminative interface made operational. It introduces no new model and reroutes the task through the judgement the backbone already performs reliably.

3.2 Framework Overview

The pipeline has three stages. A coarse scan places KcK_{c} clip centres uniformly over [0,T][0,T] and asks the frozen backbone one binary question per clip, yielding an action-probability curve. Non-maximum suppression keeps the top NpN_{p} candidate peaks, a fine scan re-examines the neighbourhood of each candidate with KfK_{f} clips, and a joint score over both scans selects the final peak t∗t^{*}. The prediction is a fixed-width window centred on t∗t^{*}. The decomposition is not plumbing but the operational form of the analysis in Sec. 5: ask the model only the question it answers reliably, consume only the ranking of its answers, and emit only the geometry the signal quality supports. Each stage exists because the corresponding shortcut fails, and Sec. 3.6 traces each choice to the failure it answers. The framework involves no training, no fine-tuning, and no temporal supervision; the only learned component is the frozen backbone itself.

3.3 Stage 1: Coarse Scanning with a Frozen Measurement Layer

Sampling. We place KcK_{c} clip centres {ti}\{t_{i}\} uniformly over [0,T][0,T]. Each clip is represented by F=5F{=}5 frames extracted symmetrically about tit_{i} and spaced δ\delta apart, where δ\delta is one third of the probe spacing, so a probe spans 4​δ4\delta; frames are resized to 448×448448{\times}448. Both settings sit at a measured optimum. Fewer frames or a narrower span lose accuracy, more frames over the same span add nothing, and a wider span hurts (Sec. 5.6). The budget KcK_{c} scales with video duration so that the spacing between probes stays within a few seconds: Kc=12K_{c}{=}12 on Charades-STA (about 30 s videos, 2.5 s spacing), Kc=16K_{c}{=}16 on ActivityNet Captions (125 s, 7.8 s), Kc=16K_{c}{=}16 on QVHighlights (150 s, 9.4 s), and Kc=96K_{c}{=}96 on TACoS (400 s, 4.2 s). This spacing rule is also where accuracy peaks: on Charades-STA both a sparser and a denser scan are worse than the deployed budget (Sec. 5.6), so the scan cannot be improved by sampling the timeline harder; what does improve it is enriching the evidence each probe sees, which is the role of the five-frame probe. Each clip receives the fixed prompt "Does this clip show {q~\tilde{q}}? Answer Yes or No.", where q~\tilde{q} is the query with trailing punctuation removed. This single template is used unchanged for every clip, query, backbone and dataset; no per-corpus prompt engineering is involved.

Probability readout. From the logits of the first generated token we compute

P⁡(Yes∣ti)=∑v∈𝒱yespv∑v∈𝒱yespv+∑v∈𝒱nopv,P(\text{Yes}\mid t_{i})=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{yes}}}p_{v}}{\displaystyle\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{yes}}}p_{v}+\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{no}}}p_{v}}, (1)

where 𝒱yes\mathcal{V}_{\text{yes}} and 𝒱no\mathcal{V}_{\text{no}} are the token sets covering the surface forms of Yes and No. No decoding beyond the first token is required. Reading position zero is safe rather than merely convenient: probing 3,6003{,}600 clips under the deployed configuration, the mass ∑𝒱yespv+∑𝒱nopv\sum_{\mathcal{V}_{\text{yes}}}p_{v}+\sum_{\mathcal{V}_{\text{no}}}p_{v} that Eq. 1 normalises by never falls below 0.9980.998, the first-token argmax is a Yes/No surface form on every clip without exception, and greedy decoding never places its answer at a later position. The denominator is therefore a normalisation over essentially all of the first-token distribution, not a renormalisation of a small residue. Downstream stages consume only the ranking of these scores across clips, never their calibrated values, so a backbone whose absolute probabilities are poorly calibrated can still be a strong scanner. The same probe makes the distinction concrete. The discrete answer is No on 88.3%88.3\% of clips even though 27.9%27.9\% of them fall inside the ground-truth interval: the median score on a positive clip is 0.2020.202 against 0.0420.042 on a negative one, so the two populations are well ordered (AUROC 0.7320.732) while both sit far below the natural decision boundary, which recovers only 26.4%26.4\% of positive clips at F1=0.368F_{1}{=}0.368. Retuning the threshold does not repair this. The optimum lies at 0.100.10 rather than 0.50.5 and still reaches only F1=0.536F_{1}{=}0.536, because the score scale drifts across videos: the tenth and ninetieth percentiles of the per-video maximum are 0.1650.165 and 0.9060.906, so any global threshold is simultaneously too strict for one video and too permissive for another. Ranking is a within-video operation and is immune to that drift; taking the per-video argmax with no threshold at all lands inside the ground-truth interval on 66.0%66.0\% of videos. A hard Yes/No readout would discard three quarters of the positive evidence and leave the scan curve nearly flat, while the continuous score preserves exactly the ordering that this conservatism destroys. The interface change therefore requires probabilities and not answers. Sec. 5 examines this distinction directly.

A pluggable measurement layer. Stage 1 treats the backbone as a measurement instrument. Nothing in the pipeline depends on its architecture, so the backbone can be exchanged freely. We instantiate it with InternVL2-8B [4], Qwen2.5-VL-7B [1], LLaVA-NeXT-Video-7B [32], and mPLUG-Owl3-7B [29], all frozen. Because per-clip discriminability is one of the two failure axes we identify, upgrading the instrument converts directly to accuracy where that axis binds: on TACoS, replacing InternVL2 with Qwen2.5-VL raises R@0.5 from 8.6 to 13.0 with the pipeline unchanged (Sec. 5).

3.4 Stage 2: Peak Localization

The coarse curve typically contains several local maxima. We keep the top NpN_{p} of them under non-maximum suppression with radius rfr_{f}: candidates are selected greedily by score, and each selection suppresses all positions within rfr_{f} seconds,

t^j=arg⁡maxti⁡P⁡(Yes∣ti)s.t.|ti−t^j′|>rf​∀j′<j.\hat{t}_{j}=\arg\max_{t_{i}}\;P(\text{Yes}\mid t_{i})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad|t_{i}-\hat{t}_{j^{\prime}}|>r_{f}\;\;\forall j^{\prime}<j. (2)

We fix Np=3N_{p}{=}3 for every corpus. The sweep in Sec. 5.6 shows the multi-candidate gain saturates by the second or third candidate on every corpus and is flat thereafter, so a single shared value suffices and no per-corpus tuning is needed. Around each candidate t^j\hat{t}_{j} a fine scan places Kf=8K_{f}{=}8 clips uniformly within [t^j−rf,t^j+rf][\hat{t}_{j}-r_{f},\,\hat{t}_{j}+r_{f}], giving scores {Pj​kf}\{P^{f}_{jk}\}, with rf=8r_{f}{=}8 s, 2525 s, 2525 s, and 3030 s on Charades-STA, ActivityNet, QVHighlights, and TACoS respectively, matching each corpus’s event scale. Candidates are then ranked by the joint score

sj=P​(Yes∣t^j)α⋅(maxk⁡Pj​kf)1−α,α=0.5,s_{j}=P(\text{Yes}\mid\hat{t}_{j})^{\,\alpha}\cdot\Bigl(\max_{k}\,P^{f}_{jk}\Bigr)^{\!1-\alpha},\qquad\alpha=0.5, (3)

a geometric mean that weighs the two scan resolutions equally and is insensitive to their absolute scales. We fix α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 rather than learning it, keeping the pipeline free of trained parameters; Sec. 5.6 shows accuracy is stable across α\alpha. The final peak t∗t^{*} is the fine-scan argmax under the winning candidate.

3.5 Stage 3: Window Generation and Its Geometric Characterisation

Output rule and the width setting. The prediction is a fixed-width window centred on the peak and truncated at the video boundary,

[s^,e^]=[max⁡(0,t∗−W/2),min⁡(T,t∗+W/2)].[\hat{s},\hat{e}]=\bigl[\max(0,\;t^{*}\!-\!W/2),\;\min(T,\;t^{*}\!+\!W/2)\bigr]. (4)

Here WW is a per-corpus expectation of event scale (88 s on Charades-STA, 2020 s on TACoS, 8080 s on ActivityNet Captions), and the one setting in the pipeline with the character of a domain prior, so we state exactly where each value comes from. On Charades-STA the deployed value is the corpus mean event length read from the training split (7.87.8 s rounded to 88), and on QVHighlights likewise (25.125.1 s rounded to 2525). On the two long-video corpora no single training statistic reproduces the deployed values, because their event distributions span two orders of magnitude and any single width is a compromise; the values sit on the broad plateau that the sensitivity sweep in Sec. 5.6 makes explicit, and the same sweep reports the cost of insisting on the strictly prior-derived alternative. As WW grows, R@0.3 rises and R@0.7 falls while R@0.5 stays within about one point across a wide band, exactly the trade that IoU=min⁡(W,g)/max⁡(W,g)\mathrm{IoU}=\min(W,g)/\max(W,g) predicts, so a choice within the plateau shifts error between thresholds rather than manufacturing accuracy. The remaining settings (KcK_{c}, rfr_{f}, NpN_{p}) follow the video’s temporal resolution and are not tuned to the target.

Geometric characterisation. The fixed window makes the attainable accuracy analytically predictable. If the peak is perfectly centred on an event of width gg, the overlap is

IoU⁡(W,g)=min⁡(W,g)max⁡(W,g),\mathrm{IoU}(W,g)=\frac{\min(W,g)}{\max(W,g)}, (5)

so IoU≥0.5\mathrm{IoU}\geq 0.5 requires g∈[W/2, 2​W]g\in[\,W/2,\;2W\,], and outside this band R@0.5 is zero regardless of how well the peak is localised. This closed form is a testable prediction, not a disclaimer: on ActivityNet the ground-truth buckets lying outside the feasible band show exactly zero R@0.5, matching the bound. Where the band is satisfied, final accuracy sits close to this geometric ceiling, indicating that post-peak error is small and that performance is governed primarily by window–event geometry (Sec. 5).

Adaptive width as a documented variant. A natural alternative sets WW per sample from the full width at half maximum of the coarse curve, clipped to a global physical guardrail of [2,120][2,120] s whose bounds reject single-probe noise spikes and prevent divergence on flat curves, and which contains no dataset statistics. This variant recovers long events that no single fixed width can cover but degrades short homogeneous events, a two-sided pattern that is stable under both an absolute and a baseline-corrected half-maximum definition. Sec. 5.6 quantifies both directions. A gating rule derived from the scan curve cannot separate the two regimes: the curve’s full width at half maximum is uncorrelated with event duration (Sec. 5), so no global threshold on it recovers the adaptive gain without reintroducing the fixed-window loss. We therefore keep the fixed window as the default.

3.6 Design Rationale: What the Two-Axis Analysis Dictates

Each design choice above follows from one of the two failure axes we measure in Sec. 5. We sample uniformly rather than adaptively focusing the scan because sampling is not the bottleneck. Under the budgets above, the analytic probability that at least one probe lands inside the ground-truth interval is 0.87 to 0.95 across the three corpora, while the measured peak hit rate is far lower, placing the loss in per-clip discrimination rather than in coverage. We predict a peak plus a window rather than estimating interval boundaries because boundary estimation demands a signal quality the per-clip scores do not provide. An interval-estimation variant based on thresholded score support underperformed peak detection consistently and is reported as a negative result in Sec. 5. Finally, we train nothing. Fine-tuning the backbone would forfeit the central claim, that the grounding ability already exists in the frozen model and is buried by the generative interface, and it would forfeit the property that FV-Action improves for free with every stronger release of its measurement layer.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets.

We evaluate on three standard TVG benchmarks. Charades-STA [7] contains 3,720 test samples from indoor activity videos (mean duration 30.6 s, mean GT length 7.8 s). ActivityNet Captions [13] is evaluated on the standard val_1 split of 17,505 query-video pairs (mean duration 180 s, mean GT length 37.7 s). As on all prior work, a fraction of the YouTube source videos are no longer retrievable, so, following common practice, evaluation is restricted to the videos that remain available; we report on this set without penalising the method for missing videos, matching the protocol used by the baselines we compare against. TACoS [23] covers 4,001 test samples from a single cooking domain (mean video duration 6.7 min), a challenging out-of-domain setting for zero-shot methods. QVHighlights [15] contains 1,550 val queries over 150 s vlog and news clips (train mean moment length 25.1 s); 34%34\% of queries annotate multiple disjoint moments, and a prediction is scored by its maximum IoU over the annotated windows. As with ActivityNet, a fraction of source videos (7%7\%) is no longer retrievable, and we evaluate on the 1,441 available queries.

Metrics.

Following standard evaluation, we report Recall at IoU threshold τ\tau (RR@τ\tau, τ∈{0.3,0.5,0.7}\tau\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7\}), which measures the fraction of predictions whose temporal IoU with the ground truth exceeds τ\tau.

Direct regression baseline. The direct baseline is held strictly identical across all backbones except for the frozen vision-language model itself, so that the interface, not the input protocol, is the only variable. For every sample we uniformly sample sixteen frames, one at the centre of each of sixteen equal temporal segments, and present them to the model under a single verbatim text prompt: the video duration in seconds, the query, and the instruction to output only the start and end time in seconds. The prompt states the duration so the model has an explicit temporal anchor; the interface, not missing time information, is what we test. The sixteen frames are ingested through each backbone’s native video interface (image tokens for InternVL2, which has no video modality, and the native video token for Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-NeXT-Video, and mPLUG-Owl3), which is the only component that differs across backbones; no per-frame timestamp markup is inserted, so no backbone is forced into an unnatural interleaved image mode. Generation is greedy with a thirty-two token budget, we parse the first two decimals in the output as [s^,e^][\hat{s},\hat{e}] clamped to [0,D][0,D], and report the standard temporal IoU, taken as the maximum over ground-truth windows. A controlled interface comparison requires the two arms to see the video at a comparable temporal resolution, which we define as the number of distinct temporal locations sampled across the clip, not the raw frame count. On Charades-STA the regression arm draws sixteen uniform frames, i.e. sixteen temporal locations, while the FV-Action coarse scan probes Kc=12K_{c}{=}12 clip centres, so the two arms cover the timeline at a similar granularity even though FV-Action reads three frames per clip (thirty-six frames total). If anything the extra frames give no coverage advantage, since they are clustered at the same twelve locations. On ActivityNet and TACoS the sixteen-frame regression input and the sixteen- or ninety-six-probe scan differ in temporal resolution by design, which would confound the interface with coverage, so we do not report a controlled regression baseline there.

Implementation details.

All backbones are used frozen, with no fine-tuning or temporal supervision at any stage. We evaluate four public checkpoints without modification: InternVL2-8B , Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, LLaVA-NeXT-Video-7B, and mPLUG-Owl3-7B. We run inference in half precision (bfloat16, or float16 for LLaVA-NeXT-Video) on a single NVIDIA A100; the full pipeline requires no training and no gradient computation. Frames are decoded with ffmpeg at 448×448448{\times}448 and, for each clip, F=3F{=}3 frames are sampled around the clip centre. The binary VQA prompt is fixed across all datasets and backbones (Sec. 3.3); P⁡(Yes)P(\text{Yes}) is read from the first-token logits over the Yes/No surface-form token sets (Eq. 1). We fix the joint-score exponent α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5. The three per-corpus settings follow each video’s temporal scale and are summarised in Table 1; no other hyperparameter is tuned to the target datasets. For the direct-regression baseline we generate greedily with a 32-token budget and parse the first two decimals as [s^,e^][\hat{s},\hat{e}]. All reported numbers use a single inference run (the pipeline is deterministic under greedy decoding).

Inference cost.

Being training-free trades gradient updates for repeated forward passes at inference. Each sample requires Kc+Np​KfK_{c}+N_{p}K_{f} binary-VQA forwards: the KcK_{c} coarse probes plus a fine scan of Kf=8K_{f}{=}8 clips around each of the NpN_{p} surviving candidates. This is 36 forwards on Charades-STA (12+3×812{+}3{\times}8), 40 on ActivityNet (16+3×816{+}3{\times}8), and 120 on TACoS (96+3×896{+}3{\times}8), against a single forward for direct regression. Each forward reads only the first-token Yes/No logits (Eq. 1), with no autoregressive decoding, and the probes are mutually independent, so they are issued as GPU batches rather than sequentially. On a shared 19.5 GB A100 MIG partition the median wall-clock cost per sample is 14.4 s, 22.4 s, and 95.6 s (Table 1); on a dedicated A100 the Charades figure falls to 10.3 s. The cost is dominated by the backbone’s forward pass, not by video decoding, and scales with the probe budget, so it is the price of avoiding any training rather than a fixed overhead: it trades a one-time training and annotation burden, which the reinforcement-learning and large-scale-SFT baselines pay, for test-time computation that needs no labels. The budget is also adjustable: reducing KcK_{c} trades accuracy for forwards along a measured curve (Sec. 5.6), and the scan inherits any speedup of the underlying backbone.

4.2 Main Results

Tables 3, 4, and 5 report results on Charades-STA, ActivityNet Captions, and TACoS respectively.

Charades-STA.

FV-Action with Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves 56.8%56.8\% R@0.5, surpassing all trained TVG VLMs including TimeMarker (51.9%51.9\%), which is trained on over one million TVG samples, and VideoChat-Flash (53.1%53.1\%). Most directly, it surpasses the same backbone’s own native temporal pipeline (Qwen2.5-VL zero-shot, 53.6%53.6\%) on identical frozen weights, and does so on the tighter R@0.7 as well (29.729.7 vs. 28.528.5): switching the interface, not the model, is what improves grounding. Among training-free methods, FV-Action improves over GranAlign (39.6%39.6\%) by 17.217.2 pp, despite GranAlign relying on a multi-model pipeline with LLM rewriting and CLIP matching. It remains competitive with systems that pay for reinforcement learning or large-scale SFT, trailing Time-R1 (60.8%60.8\%, RL on 2,500 grounding samples) and OmniVTG [33] (63.2%63.2\%, 359,K annotations over 2,124 hours), while using no temporal training of any kind. The interface comparison in Table 6 shows that every tested backbone benefits from the VQA interface, with gains from +28+28 to +50+50 pp.

ActivityNet Captions.

FV-Action achieves 26.7%26.7\% R@0.5 with Qwen2.5-VL and 25.5%25.5\% with both InternVL2-8B and LLaVA-NeXT-Video, surpassing ChatVTG (22.5%22.5\%), Momentor (23.0%23.0\%), and UniTime (22.8%22.8\%), while trailing VTimeLLM (29.5%29.5\%) and HawkEye (29.3%29.3\%), both fine-tuned on temporal grounding data. The result is stable across the two annotation splits of ActivityNet: the Qwen2.5-VL R@0.5 is 26.7%26.7\% on val_1 and 27.0%27.0\% on val_2. Among multi-model training-free methods, GranAlign (34.0%34.0\%) and BTDP (30.6%30.6\%) outperform FV-Action on R@0.5; both use multi-stage pipelines with dense captioners and LLM alignment, whereas FV-Action uses only a single VLM query. ActivityNet is also where the adaptive-window variant helps most: it lifts InternVL2 to 29.8%29.8\% (Sec. 5.6), reflecting the dataset’s heterogeneous event durations. The primary failure mode under the fixed window is a window/short-GT mismatch: 38%38\% of queries have GT shorter than 15 s, yet the window is 80 s, causing structural failures on short events regardless of peak-localization quality.

QVHighlights.

FV-Action reaches 43.043.0 R1@0.5 and 16.716.7 R1@0.7 on the val split (72.972.9 R@0.3, mIoU 45.245.2; Table 2), 1.7×1.7\times the zero-shot pretraining transfer of UniVTG (25.225.2) and within eleven points of the fully supervised Moment-DETR (53.953.9), with no exposure to any moment-retrieval data. The multi-model pipeline GranAlign is substantially stronger here (61.961.9), the reverse of the Charades-STA ordering, and the gap is concentrated at the tight threshold (41.841.8 vs 16.716.7 R1@0.7) where our single fixed 2525 s width faces moments ranging from seconds to a minute; QVHighlights is thus the corpus where the geometry axis costs a single-model scan the most, exactly as the two-axis account predicts. Perception, in contrast, is our strongest of the four benchmarks: the selected peak lands inside an annotated moment on 77.3%77.3\% of queries.

TACoS.

FV-Action with Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves 29.5%29.5\% R@0.3 and 13.0%13.0\% R@0.5 on TACoS, a domain that all compared methods encounter zero-shot. FV-Action outperforms all trained TVG VLMs on this benchmark, surpassing ChatVTG (3.7%3.7\%), VTimeLLM (3.9%3.9\%), ED-VTG (6.0%6.0\%), and UniTime (7.4%7.4\%) by 5.75.7–9.49.4 pp. The InternVL2 backbone (8.6%8.6\%) already exceeds all prior methods; Qwen2.5-VL provides an additional +4.6+4.6 pp, reflecting stronger clip-level discriminability. TACoS remains the hardest setting for FV-Action: long cooking videos (mean 6.7 min) spread the coarse scan thin, while short GT events compound the fixed-window mismatch.

4.3 The Interface Bottleneck

Same model, different interface.

Table 6 isolates the effect of task formulation. Both interfaces are training-free and use identical input, sixteen uniformly sampled frames with a simple zero-shot prompt, no model-specific temporal encoding and no TVG supervision; the only variable is whether the model emits timestamps or answers a binary VQA query. Across every backbone the VQA interface outperforms timestamp regression by 2828–5050 pp in R@0.5. InternVL2-8B rises from 3.763.76 under regression to 53.3953.39 with scanning: under the generative interface it degenerates to emitting the whole video ([0,T][0,T]), which reaches R@0.3 by trivial coverage but almost never R@0.5, even though its clip-level discriminability reaches AUROC 0.7820.782 on the same frames, so the missing ingredient is not perception but the output channel. LLaVA-NeXT-Video-7B is the extreme case: under regression it fails to emit two parseable timestamps on 69%69\% of samples, so scored strictly its R@0.5 is 0.050.05, yet the same frozen backbone recovers to 47.0447.04 with scanning. Qwen2.5-VL-7B rises from 28.4128.41 to 56.7756.77. Because the backbone is frozen and only the output format changes, this gap identifies the interface as the cause. The comparison is sharpest against the native dense temporal pipeline of Qwen2.5-VL (53.653.6 R@0.5 [33]): on the same weights, FV-Action exceeds it on both R@0.5 (56.856.8) and R@0.7 (29.729.7 vs. 28.528.5) using only sixteen frames and no temporal machinery.

Is the regression baseline under-prompted?

A gap this large invites the objection that the direct baseline simply received a poor prompt. Table 7 answers it by sweeping five prompt formulations for Qwen2.5-VL under the regression interface, holding frames, decoding and parser fixed, on a common 400400-sample subset. The prompt deployed in Table 6, which states the video duration, is the best of the five and is reproduced by variant V1 to within half a point of R@0.5. Withholding the duration (V0) costs 9.89.8 pp, and the two formulations that supply the model with more temporal scaffolding are the two that hurt most: per-frame timestamps in the text (V2) drop format compliance to 66.8%66.8\%, and chain-of-thought reasoning before the answer (V3) destroys it entirely, with no sample in the subset emitting a parseable interval. The deployed baseline therefore sits at the maximum of this family rather than below it, and the residual gap to VQA scanning is not a prompting artefact. The V3 result is the sharpest form of the interface problem: asking the model to reason about time is precisely what stops it from reporting time in a format anyone can read.

Is the scanning interface prompt-sensitive too?

The converse question is whether the VQA arm merely hides its own prompt sensitivity. Table 8 answers it by rewriting the scan question five ways under a frozen pipeline, on the same 400400-sample subset. The spread is 3.23.2 pp R@0.5 between the best and worst formulation, against 18.518.5 pp on the regression side of Table 7. We state what this subset can and cannot establish. At n=400n{=}400 the paired McNemar test resolves differences of about 55 pp, so the result bounds the effect rather than excluding it: no rewriting we tried moves R@0.5 by the double-digit margin that separates the two interfaces, but a small effect would not be visible here. The largest gain on the subset, dropping the Answer Yes or No suffix (S5), was +2.0+2.0 pp R@0.5 but with a 95%95\% confidence interval of [−1.5,+5.5][-1.5,+5.5]; re-running S5 against a paired baseline on the full 3,7203{,}720 samples, where the test resolves 1.71.7 pp, collapses it to −0.4-0.4 pp R@0.5 (p=0.57p{=}0.57) and 0.00.0 pp R@0.7 (p=1.0p{=}1.0). The apparent subset gain was sampling noise, and we keep the deployed prompt. One hypothesis is settled rather than merely unresolved. Charades queries begin with a bare person on 57.5%57.5\% of samples, so the deployed template produces ungrammatical questions (“Does this clip show person turn a light on?”). Repairing the article perturbs the scan curve on every one of those samples, yet the argmax survives on 81.3%81.3\% of them and R@0.5 and peak-in-GT are numerically identical, with only 88 of 400400 samples crossing the R@0.5 threshold in either direction (confidence interval [−1.5,+1.5][-1.5,+1.5]). Here the tight interval does license the negative reading: grammar shifts the scores without reordering them, and the scan consumes only the order. We also let the backbone rewrite its own question rather than relying on our hand-written variants (S6): Qwen2.5-VL is prompted to turn each query into a clean binary question, which it does with no format failures, and the pipeline runs on the result. This does not help either, and mildly hurts R@0.7 (−4.3-4.3 pp, p=0.06p{=}0.06, against a paired baseline of 32.832.8), because the rewrites tend to over-specify a loosely annotated action; even an automated search over phrasings finds no headroom. That mechanism is the interface claim restated. Ranking absorbs perturbations that would corrupt a generated string, which is why phrasing costs the scan at most a few points while the same backbone asked to emit timestamps swings by 18.518.5 pp on wording alone. We note that the two sweeps are not perturbations of equal severity: the regression variants include structural changes such as interleaved per-frame timestamps and chain-of-thought, whereas the scan variants are rewordings of a fixed question, since the binary format admits no structural analogue.

Backbone generality.

The interface gain is not a property of one model. Table 6 shows all four backbones, spanning four architectures, improving by 2828 to 5050 pp R@0.5 over their own regression baselines under the identical frozen pipeline, with the backbone ordering preserved across the switch.

5 Analysis: Two Axes of Failure

Where FV-Action still fails, the failures decompose along two measurable and separable axes: a perception axis governed by the backbone’s per-clip discriminability, and a geometry axis governed by the fixed output window. Figure 2 shows one example of each regime. We characterise each axis, show they are separable, turn the perception axis into a pre-deployment diagnostic, catalogue the alternatives that do not work, and close with component ablations.

5.1 The Perception Axis: Backbone-Dependent Discriminability

Oracle protocol.

For each sample we take the ground-truth interval as a positive clip and an equal-width non-overlapping window from the same video as a negative, and record the signal gap Δ=P⁡(Yes∣GT)−P⁡(Yes∣neg)\Delta=P(\text{Yes}\mid\text{GT})-P(\text{Yes}\mid\text{neg}) and the discrimination rate disc=P⁡(pgt>pneg)\mathrm{disc}=P(p_{\text{gt}}>p_{\text{neg}}). This measures per-clip separability, what the scan actually consumes, independent of any localisation machinery.

The axis moves with the backbone.

On TACoS the oracle gap rises from 0.1860.186 (InternVL2) to 0.2600.260 (Qwen2.5-VL), a paired difference on identical samples (n=200n{=}200, p=0.0009p{=}0.0009), and pipeline R@0.5 rises with it from 8.68.6 to 13.013.0 with nothing else changed. Entropy offers no comparable handle: it discriminates correct from incorrect predictions at AUROC 0.5390.539–0.5780.578 across TimeChat, LITA, and VTG-LLM, near chance, whereas the clip-level VQA probability reaches AUROC 0.7820.782 on InternVL2-8B, which is why entropy-gated correction reaches only sub-random F1 (below 0.360.36) while VQA scanning succeeds.

Ranking, not calibration.

On TACoS, Qwen2.5-VL answers the oracle question correctly on only 32.5%32.5\% of ground-truth clips (p¯gt=0.372\bar{p}_{\text{gt}}=0.372), yet its discrimination rate is 80.5%80.5\% because negatives sit on a clean low baseline (p¯neg=0.112\bar{p}_{\text{neg}}=0.112). A backbone can therefore appear poorly calibrated in isolation and still be a strong scanner, precisely the property the pipeline consumes (Sec. 3.3).

The residual sits on the perception axis, not the pipeline.

A natural question is whether smarter curve processing could recover the located peak where it currently misses. On Charades-STA the peak lands inside the ground truth on 67.7%67.7\% of samples, and among the failures 65.6%65.6\% have the best in-interval clip ranked within the coarse top three, which would suggest a ceiling of 88.8%88.8\% peak accuracy if a selection rule could exploit it. That headroom is illusory. The wrong peak beats the best in-interval clip by a median of only 0.0930.093 in P⁡(Yes)P(\text{Yes}): the errors are small-margin perception noise, not a systematic bias a filter can subtract. Accordingly, every curve-level remedy we tried lowers accuracy rather than raising it. Temporal smoothing of the coarse curve drops peak accuracy to 62.4%62.4\% and R@0.5 to 52.652.6; contrastive scoring, which subtracts a background-query probability to suppress scene bias, drops them to 62.4%62.4\% and 54.154.1; doubling the probe budget and rewording the question leave both unchanged (Sec. 5.6, Table 8). What does move peak accuracy is the backbone: on the identical pipeline it rises monotonically 50.9→57.0→63.1→67.7%50.9\rightarrow 57.0\rightarrow 63.1\rightarrow 67.7\% across mPLUG-Owl3, LLaVA-NeXT-Video, InternVL2, and Qwen2.5-VL, tracking their R@0.5 order. The two-axis account is therefore not only descriptive but prescriptive: with geometry handled by the window prior, the remaining error is a property of per-clip discriminability, and the operative lever is a stronger instrument, not a cleverer read of a fixed one.

5.2 The Geometry Axis: Analytically Predictable Coverage

Eq. (5) implies a feasible band g∈[W/2, 2​W]g\in[W/2,\,2W] outside of which R@0.5 is zero for a perfectly placed window. Figure 3 tests this on ActivityNet at W=80W{=}80 s: buckets with ground truth shorter than 4040 s collapse to 33–24%24\% exactly as the bound dictates, with the small residuals explained by boundary truncation, while buckets inside the band reach 5050–56%56\%. Figure 4 separates the two axes on the same data: for gg between 4545 and 110110 s the peak ceiling holds at 9292–95%95\%, so perception has already succeeded and the gap to the actual 5050–56%56\% is entirely the window’s inability to express the found peak. Aggregating over all six dataset and backbone combinations, the peak ceiling predicts final R@0.5 with r=0.998r=0.998 (Fig. 5); the residual to the diagonal is the geometry loss.

The adaptive-width variant is the direct response to this axis. Table 9 shows its per-bucket effect on ActivityNet with Qwen2.5-VL: adaptation gains 1010–1818 pp on both tails (g<30g<30 s and g>110g>110 s) where the fixed width mismatches the event, and loses 1212–2121 pp on the matched middle, for a net +3.4+3.4 pp; the pattern is stable under both an absolute and a baseline-corrected half-maximum definition. A remedy for the geometry axis thus exists but carries a two-sided trade-off (Sec. 5.5).

5.3 Axis Separability

Three observations establish that the two axes are independent. First, geometry can fail while perception is intact: on the mid and long ActivityNet buckets the peak ceiling holds at 9292–95%95\% while actual accuracy is 5050–56%56\% (Fig. 4). Second, when perception is equivalent, geometry decides. An earlier snapshot of our results appeared to show InternVL2 ahead of Qwen2.5-VL on ActivityNet (29.829.8 vs. 24.524.5), but the two runs used different window policies (an adaptive width against a fixed W=38W{=}38 s); under the same fixed W=80W{=}80 s the ordering reverses (25.525.5 vs. 26.726.7), and under the same adaptive variant the two fall within one point (29.229.2 vs. 30.230.2). The apparent backbone gap was a window-policy artefact. Third, when perception fails, geometry cannot compensate. On TACoS the analytic probability that some probe lands in the ground truth is 0.910.91 at Kc=96K_{c}{=}96, yet the measured peak hit rate is only 2727–39%39\%: the probes reach the event but per-clip scores do not lift it above the noise peaks, and no window rule can recover a peak that was never selected.

5.4 Predicting Deployment: The Oracle-Gap Diagnostic

The oracle gap of Sec. 5.1 is measured from two hundred clips with no localisation, making it a cheap pre-deployment probe of the perception axis. Where that axis binds, the gap predicts which backbone will deploy better: on TACoS the gap ordering (InternVL2 0.186<0.186< Qwen2.5-VL 0.2600.260) matches the deployed ordering (8.6<13.08.6<13.0) before the full pipeline is ever run. Two scope conditions keep the probe honest. First, it predicts only in the perception-limited regime; where geometry binds instead, as on Charades-STA where both backbones already discriminate above 73%73\%, the gap does not determine R@0.5 and the peak ceiling of Sec. 5.2 does. Second, the gap does not transfer across datasets: it inflates with the clip-to-event width ratio, and re-measuring it at each pipeline’s deployment clip width raises the cross-dataset correlation with the peak ceiling only to r=0.47r{=}0.47 (p=0.43p{=}0.43, n=5n{=}5). The gap is therefore a within-dataset diagnostic for the perception axis, and its failure to transfer is itself evidence for the two-axis decomposition: no single scalar predicts deployment because two independent axes govern it.

5.5 What Does Not Work

Table 10 compiles the alternatives we tested and rejected; each eliminated a hypothesis and shaped one design choice. The most consequential is the curve-derived gating rule that would apply the adaptive width of Sec. 5.2 only where it helps: because a clip’s scan-curve width (its full width at half maximum) is uncorrelated with the event duration gg, no global threshold recovers the adaptive gain without reintroducing the fixed-window loss, and the three datasets demand opposite thresholds. The event width is simply not encoded in the per-clip signal, which is why the geometry axis cannot be closed from the curve and the fixed window remains the default. A second result explains why the coarse scan places its probes uniformly rather than at visually salient instants. Replacing the uniform clip centres with content-adaptive key frames, chosen as the largest inter-frame differences so that no extra model is introduced, costs 13.113.1 pp R@0.5 on Charades-STA (43.743.7 vs. 56.856.8) and drops the fraction of peaks landing inside the ground-truth interval from 67.7%67.7\% to 53.7%53.7\%, on identical samples and an otherwise identical pipeline. Large visual change marks camera motion and lighting shifts as readily as action onsets, so key-frame selection spends the probe budget on the wrong instants. Given a fixed budget and no reliable prior over where the event lies, spreading probes uniformly is the better strategy, and the fine scan then buys locality where a coarse peak has already been found.

5.6 Ablations

Table 11 changes one component at a time under the main configuration. Removing the fine scan (localising with the coarse argmax alone) costs 1.21.2 pp on Charades but is neutral to slightly positive on TACoS and ActivityNet, where the coarse grid is already dense relative to the event scale; the fine scan earns its place on short-video corpora. Replacing the fixed window with the adaptive FWHM variant reproduces the two-sided behaviour of Sec. 5.2: a large loss on Charades and gains on TACoS and ActivityNet. Swapping the backbone from Qwen2.5-VL to InternVL2-8B moves every dataset, most strongly TACoS, which Sec. 5.1 traces to per-clip discriminability.

The remaining settings divide into two families with opposite verdicts. Two input-evidence choices, the frames each probe reads and the resolution it reads them at, genuinely move accuracy, and we report them first. Every algorithmic setting after that sits on a measured plateau, which is the quantitative form of the claim that nothing in the pipeline is tuned to the test set.

Frames per probe.

Every configuration above reads F=3F{=}3 frames per probe, a default inherited from the first prototype and, like the prompt wording, never revisited. Sweeping it exposes the one Stage-1 setting that does move localisation quality at a fixed backbone. Raising FF to five frames while widening the probe’s temporal extent from 2​δ2\delta to 4​δ4\delta, where δ\delta is one third of the probe spacing, and extracting frames symmetrically about the probe centre improves every metric on the full Charades-STA test set: R@0.5 rises from 56.756.7 to 62.362.3 (+5.7+5.7 pp, paired p=1.4×10−12p{=}1.4\times 10^{-12}, n=3720n{=}3720), R@0.7 from 29.529.5 to 31.931.9 (p=1.1×10−3p{=}1.1\times 10^{-3}), and the peak-hit rate from 67.4%67.4\% to 72.7%72.7\% (p=8×10−13p{=}8\times 10^{-13}). The two ingredients contribute separately. Five frames at the unchanged extent gain +2.6+2.6 pp R@0.5 (p=1.2×10−3p{=}1.2\times 10^{-3}), and widening the extent adds a further +3.1+3.1 pp (p=6×10−5p{=}6\times 10^{-5}). Unlike every transformation of the score curve tested in Section 5.1, this lever changes the evidence each probe sees rather than how the curve is post-processed, which is exactly where the peak-hit diagnosis says the remaining headroom lies.

The gain has a sweet spot on both sides. Eight frames over the same 4​δ4\delta extent change nothing (largest |Δ||\Delta| of 1.01.0 pp across all thresholds, none significant, full test set), so evidence saturates once within-probe frame spacing reaches the sub-second scale. Eight frames spread over 7​δ7\delta hurt (−2.6-2.6 pp R@0.5, −4.1-4.1 pp R@0.7, both p≤8×10−4p{\leq}8\times 10^{-4}), as the probe’s span grows toward the output-window width and off-event frames dilute the judgement.

The effect generalises with a magnitude that tracks how much of an event a probe can cover (Table 12). At F=5F{=}5 the within-probe frame spacing is 0.850.85 s on Charades, 1.11.1 s on TACoS, and 2.62.6 s on ActivityNet (median-length videos, deployed KcK_{c}). Charades events, with a mean length of 7.87.8 s, are the best matched to the enriched probes and gain the most; TACoS gains substantially on R@0.3 and R@0.5; ActivityNet, whose minute-scale events already exceed any probe span and whose residual sits on the geometry axis, gains least, yet the improvement remains significant at n=17,373n{=}17{,}373 and no dataset regresses on any threshold.

Input resolution.

The extra frames also change where the compute budget is best spent. All runs so far use 4482448^{2} inputs, and since vision tokens scale with pixel count, resolution is the largest cost knob after KcK_{c}. At F=3F{=}3 it cannot be turned down safely: dropping to 2242224^{2} costs 6.06.0 pp R@0.5 (paired p=0.037p{=}0.037, n=400n{=}400). At F=5F{=}5 the additional frames absorb most, but not all, of the loss. On the full test set (n=3720n{=}3720) the drop to 2242224^{2} still costs about two points on every threshold (−2.4-2.4 pp R@0.5, −1.6-1.6 pp R@0.7, all p<0.02p{<}0.02), while 3362336^{2} stays within 1.31.3 pp of 4482448^{2} with no significant difference on any threshold (closest p=0.053p{=}0.053 at R@0.7). A 400400-sample pilot had suggested 2242224^{2} was free; the full set overturns that reading, which is why we treat subset results as bounds rather than verdicts. We keep 4482448^{2} as the deployed resolution. The speed option remains real: 2242224^{2} at F=5F{=}5 runs at 62%62\% of the 4482448^{2}, F=3F{=}3 latency yet still exceeds that deployment by 3.33.3 pp R@0.5, so when latency dominates, resolution is the right knob to turn precisely because the five-frame probes absorb most of the cost.

The remaining paragraphs sweep every other setting in the pipeline. The through-line is uniform: each sits on a plateau, the deployed value lies on it, and where a nominally better point exists it is statistically indistinguishable, so we keep the prior-derived or default choice.

Joint-score weighting.

The joint score combines the coarse and fine evidence as a geometric mean with weight α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5. Recomputing peak selection offline over the stored candidate curves for α∈{0,0.1,…,1}\alpha\in\{0,0.1,\ldots,1\} on the full Charades-STA test set traces a single smooth plateau rather than a knife edge. R@0.5 is flat within 0.30.3 pp for α∈[0.3,0.6]\alpha\in[0.3,0.6], the nominal maximum at α=0.4\alpha{=}0.4 (57.0257.02) is not distinguishable from the deployed α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 (56.7556.75; paired p≥0.14p{\geq}0.14 on every threshold), and both endpoints lose about 1.21.2 to 1.51.5 pp (α=0\alpha{=}0 keeps only the fine scan, 55.5655.56; α=1\alpha{=}1 keeps only the coarse score, 55.5155.51). Combining the two resolutions is therefore load-bearing, while the balance between them is not a sensitive choice, and the untuned equal weighting sits on the plateau.

Peak readout.

Two further implicit choices sit in how the peak is read from the winning candidate’s fine curve, and neither had been varied before. Replacing the maximum fine score in the joint score with the mean or the top-two mean does not help (the mean is slightly worse, −0.8-0.8 pp R@0.3, p=0.018p{=}0.018), so the deployed maximum stands. Replacing the discrete argmax of the fine curve with a three-point parabolic interpolation around it, a parameter-free refinement with no additional forwards, raises R@0.5 by 1.161.16 pp and R@0.7 by 1.181.18 pp (both p<0.001p{<}0.001, n=3720n{=}3720, offline recomputation over the stored fine curves). The mechanism is quantisation: fine probes sit on a grid of roughly two-second spacing, the argmax returns a grid point, and sub-grid interpolation recovers part of the placement loss, which is why the gain concentrates at the tight thresholds. A score-weighted centroid of the whole curve gains more at loose thresholds (+2.4+2.4 pp R@0.5) but nothing at R@0.7 and introduces a baseline-subtraction choice, so we prefer the interpolation.

Window sensitivity.

WW is the only exposed hyperparameter, so we sweep it around each deployed value with the peak location fixed (Table 13). The pattern is the one the geometry of Eq. 5 predicts, not flat insensitivity. On the primary metric R@0.5 accuracy stays within about two points of its peak across a band around the chosen WW, and the band is widest on ActivityNet, whose long, heterogeneous events make overlap least sensitive to WW. The looser thresholds move in opposite directions: enlarging WW past the event length raises R@0.3 and lowers R@0.7, because a wider window trades boundary tightness for coverage exactly as IoU=min⁡(W,g)/max⁡(W,g)\mathrm{IoU}=\min(W,g)/\max(W,g) dictates. On Charades-STA the deployed W=8W{=}8 is the training-split mean event length, deliberately not the R@0.5-maximising width (near 1010 s), so no value is tuned on test accuracy there. The long-video corpora do not admit such a clean prior, and the sweep quantifies what insisting on one would cost. Setting WW to the training mean event length gives 35.535.5 s on ActivityNet and 3232 s on TACoS; the first loses 3.13.1 pp R@0.5 against the deployed 8080 s (26.7→23.626.7\rightarrow 23.6, paired p<10−18p{<}10^{-18}, recomputed offline with peaks fixed), and the second reads off the table as a loss of about 1.71.7 pp against the deployed 2020 s. A single width simply cannot summarise event distributions whose quartiles span two orders of magnitude, which is the geometry axis restated; the deployed values are scale choices on the plateau of Table 13, and the plateau itself is what makes them defensible.

Number of candidate peaks.

Table 14 sweeps the NMS candidate budget NpN_{p} with peak selection and window fixed. On Charades-STA the multi-candidate design earns its first two slots and then saturates exactly: R@0.5 rises from 55.555.5 (Np=1N_{p}{=}1, a single coarse peak) to 56.656.6 (Np=2N_{p}{=}2) to 56.856.8 (Np=3N_{p}{=}3), after which Np=4,5,6N_{p}{=}4,5,6 are identical to two decimals and no fourth candidate ever wins the joint score, even though 22%22\% of clips expose one. ActivityNet behaves identically, saturating by Np=2N_{p}{=}2 (26.4→26.726.4\rightarrow 26.7) and flat to Np=6N_{p}{=}6 on all three thresholds. TACoS shows no systematic trend at all: its R@0.5 fluctuates non-monotonically within 0.50.5 pp across the whole range Np∈[2,10]N_{p}\in[2,10], which we read as noise rather than signal. We therefore fix a single Np=3N_{p}{=}3 for every corpus, the saturation point of the two corpora whose behaviour is monotone. We do not select NpN_{p} per corpus: Np=2N_{p}{=}2 would be marginally better on TACoS (+0.5+0.5 pp) and marginally worse on Charades (−0.1-0.1 pp), but choosing it would amount to tuning on test accuracy, the same discipline we apply to WW (Sec. 3.5), which we also set from a training statistic rather than its test optimum. The table quantifies the cost of that discipline: under 0.50.5 pp on every corpus and every threshold.

Probe budget.

The coarse budget KcK_{c} is the one setting that also determines cost, since it dominates the Kc+Np​KfK_{c}+N_{p}K_{f} forwards per sample. Halving and doubling it on Charades-STA (Table 15) shows the deployed Kc=12K_{c}{=}12 is a maximum rather than a point on a monotone curve: Kc=8K_{c}{=}8 loses 1.11.1 pp R@0.5 while saving 11%11\% of the forwards, but Kc=24K_{c}{=}24 also loses 0.80.8 pp while costing 33%33\% more. Denser probing does not help because the corpus’s mean event lasts 7.87.8 s: at Kc=12K_{c}{=}12 the 2.62.6 s spacing already places about three probes inside the average event, and halving the spacing to 1.31.3 s mostly adds near-duplicate clips, which raises the chance that the arg-max lands on a spurious peak. The peak-hit rate moves with accuracy in both directions (65.7%65.7\%, 67.7%67.7\%, 66.3%66.3\%), confirming that the effect is localisation quality rather than window geometry. Two consequences follow: the scan cannot be made more accurate simply by sampling harder, and a cheaper operating point is available at a bounded, quantified cost.

The same test on ActivityNet rules out the natural objection that our weakest corpus is simply under-sampled. Doubling the budget there from the deployed Kc=16K_{c}{=}16 to 3232 leaves all three thresholds unmoved on the full 17,37317{,}373 pairs (48.63→48.6048.63\rightarrow 48.60, 26.69→26.4726.69\rightarrow 26.47, 11.90→11.8311.90\rightarrow 11.83; paired McNemar p=0.93p{=}0.93, 0.390.39, 0.750.75), and the peak-hit rate rises by only 0.140.14 pp. Stratifying by event length locates the reason. Events shorter than 3030 s, which are 59%59\% of the corpus and where peaks land inside the ground truth only 45.8%45.8\% of the time, gain 0.40.4 pp of peak-hit from twice the probes, while events longer than 8080 s lose 2.62.6 pp R@0.5 as the extra candidates admit more spurious peaks. Short events are missed because the backbone does not discriminate them at any spacing we can afford, not because the scan steps over them, which places the residual ActivityNet gap on the perception axis rather than the sampling budget.

Fine-scan settings.

The fine stage has two settings of its own, the clip count Kf=8K_{f}{=}8 and the radius rfr_{f}, which also serves as the NMS suppression radius; like the frame count above, neither had previously been varied. Halving or doubling either one (Kf∈{4,16}K_{f}\in\{4,16\}, rf∈{4,16}r_{f}\in\{4,16\} s on Charades-STA, pipeline otherwise frozen, paired on a 400400-sample subset) moves no threshold significantly (largest |Δ||\Delta| of 4.04.0 pp, smallest p=0.12p{=}0.12). The subset resolves only effects above roughly five points, so it bounds the sensitivity rather than excluding smaller effects, but a large hidden optimum is unlikely given that the fine scan’s entire contribution is 1.21.2 pp (Table 11). The deployed Kf=8K_{f}{=}8, rf=8r_{f}{=}8 therefore stand; we note that Kf=4K_{f}{=}4 matches the baseline within noise at roughly half the per-sample cost (7.27.2 vs 13.713.7 s median), a candidate operating point for latency-sensitive deployments.

6 Conclusion

We asked why multimodal LLMs that demonstrably see an event cannot say when it happens. The answer is not ignorance. Their timestamp errors are confident, entropy-based detection performs below a random classifier, and the same frozen weights that regress timestamps at single-digit accuracy discriminate event clips reliably when asked a binary question. The failure lives in the interface, and replacing regression with a coarse-to-fine scan of binary questions recovers 2828 to 5050 R@0.5 points across four backbones without training anything. The residual failures decompose along two measurable axes, a perception axis that moves with the backbone and a geometry axis that is analytically predictable from the fit between the output window and the event width, and this decomposition is prescriptive. It tells a practitioner, before deployment, whether a corpus needs a stronger instrument or a better output rule, and it locates FV-Action’s remaining errors precisely. The resulting system reaches 56.8%56.8\% R@0.5 on Charades-STA, above the same backbone’s native temporal pipeline and above all prior training-free methods, while remaining a frozen model asked nothing but yes-or-no questions.

Limitations.

FV-Action trades training for test-time computation: 3636 to 120120 forwards per sample against one for direct regression, a cost that scales with the probe budget and inherits any speedup of the backbone, but that is real in latency-critical settings. The geometry axis is managed rather than solved. A fixed window cannot summarise corpora whose event lengths span two orders of magnitude, which is why ActivityNet remains our weakest benchmark; curve-derived adaptive widths provably do not close this gap, and conditioning the width on the query text is the direction our analysis points to. Compound queries that describe several events remain out of scope, since sub-event peaks do not separate on the scan curve. Finally, the scan is only as good as the backbone’s binary judgement. Brief events inside long videos remain under-discriminated at any probe spacing we can afford, and a backbone that answers uniformly across a video contributes no ranking signal at all. The dependence cuts both ways: every improvement in frozen VLMs’ per-clip discrimination converts directly into grounding accuracy, with no retraining, which is precisely the property a training-free method should have.
